title: Lesson 7: Moving Forward After Disagreements
summary: Restore professional cooperation after a resolved issue. You do not need to become friends, but you must keep communicating, stay accountable and avoid retaliation.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Letting go of resentment, rebuilding trust, accountability after apologies and the MOVE method

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Two therapists have a disagreement about shared responsibilities. They discuss the issue with their supervisor. The responsibilities are clarified. Both employees acknowledge their part in the misunderstanding. The immediate problem is resolved.
However, one therapist continues avoiding the other. She refuses to greet her. She makes sarcastic comments. She tells other employees: "I've forgiven her, but I'll never help her again."
The disagreement may have been formally addressed, but the working relationship remains strained.

Moving forward means allowing an appropriately resolved issue to stop interfering unnecessarily with professional behaviour, while maintaining accountability, reasonable boundaries and any agreed improvements.
It does not require pretending that nothing happened. It does not require becoming close friends. It requires employees to restore appropriate professional cooperation.

sections.title: 2. Why moving forward matters
paragraphs: A disagreement should not continue affecting work long after the underlying issue has been appropriately addressed.

sections.title: 3. Resolution is not the same as pretending
paragraphs: Employees sometimes try to move forward by avoiding the issue entirely. For example: "Let's just forget it."
However, if the original problem remains unresolved, it may happen again.
Moving forward works best when the underlying issue has been addressed, not merely ignored.

sections.title: 4. Let go of unnecessary resentment
paragraphs: After a disagreement, an employee may continue replaying the conversation mentally.
She may think: "I can't believe she spoke to me like that." "Next time she needs help, I'll show her." "She embarrassed me, so I'll embarrass her too."
These thoughts can encourage retaliation.
Employees should avoid allowing past disagreements to determine how they treat colleagues in unrelated situations.

sections.title: 5. Do not punish colleagues through silence or exclusion
paragraphs: Employees do not have to become personal friends after a disagreement. However, they should continue necessary professional communication.

Example: A receptionist and therapist disagree about a booking. After the issue is resolved, the receptionist deliberately refuses to communicate future appointment changes to the therapist. This is unacceptable because it interferes with work.
Professional alternative: The employees may keep their interactions brief and work-focused while continuing to exchange all necessary information respectfully.
Professional cooperation is required even when personal closeness is absent.

sections.title: 6. Rebuilding trust takes consistent behaviour
paragraphs: Trust may not return immediately after a serious disagreement.
Employees should not demand instant trust from someone who has experienced repeated problems.
Trust is strengthened by repeated actions, not promises alone.

Example: A therapist repeatedly fails to complete a shared task. After the issue is resolved, she begins completing the task consistently. Over time, her colleagues gain confidence in her reliability.

sections.title: 7. The difference between forgiveness and accountability
paragraphs: An employee may decide not to hold personal resentment toward a colleague. However, this does not mean repeated misconduct should be ignored.
For example, an employee may accept a colleague's apology while still expecting the agreed procedure to be followed.
Likewise, serious misconduct may still require appropriate investigation or action.
Moving forward does not cancel accountability. It means avoiding unnecessary hostility while allowing appropriate corrective steps to take effect.

sections.title: 8. Avoid bringing old disagreements into every new issue
paragraphs: Two therapists previously disagreed about a handover. Several weeks later, one asks the other to clarify a booking. The colleague responds: "You're asking me questions now? Remember how you treated me last month?"
This introduces an old dispute into an unrelated conversation.
Better response: "The booking is scheduled for 4 p.m. Let me confirm the details."
If the earlier issue remains unresolved, it should be addressed through an appropriate separate discussion.

items.label: M — Make sure the issue is addressed
items.body: Clarify what happened and any necessary corrective action.

items.label: O — Own your responsibility
items.body: Acknowledge your part in the disagreement and correct relevant mistakes.

items.label: V — Value professional cooperation
items.body: Continue treating colleagues respectfully and fulfilling shared responsibilities.

items.label: E — Establish better habits
items.body: Apply the lessons learned and avoid repeating the behaviour that caused the conflict.

sections.title: 10. How to behave after an apology
paragraphs: If a colleague has apologised sincerely and the issue has been appropriately addressed, employees should avoid using the apology as a continuing opportunity to embarrass the person.
Do not repeatedly say: "Remember when you made that mistake?" "You should be grateful I forgave you." "Everybody knows what you did."
These comments can undermine reconciliation.
Where the conduct was serious or repeated, appropriate boundaries and formal processes may still be necessary.

sections.title: 11. How to work with someone you do not personally like
paragraphs: Professionalism does not require personal affection.

Example: Two employees do not naturally get along. However, they continue to coordinate appointments, share operational information and treat clients professionally. This demonstrates workplace maturity.

sections.title: 12. Recognising when a disagreement is not truly resolved
paragraphs: When these problems continue, further supervisory or management intervention may be necessary.
Moving forward should not be used to pressure someone into ignoring serious unresolved conduct.
list: Repeated arguments about the same issue.

sections.title: 13. Lesson 7 case study
paragraphs: Two therapists resolve a disagreement about room preparation. One apologises. However, the other continues excluding her from relevant work communication.
Expected lesson: Moving forward requires professional behaviour, not necessarily personal friendship.
list: Does accepting an apology require becoming close friends?
What responsibilities should both employees continue fulfilling?
When might supervisory follow-up be appropriate?

sections.title: 14. Practical exercise: What does moving forward look like?
table: A colleague apologises for a genuine mistake
Acknowledge the apology and focus on the agreed improvement
Two employees are no longer close after a disagreement
An old disagreement is mentioned during an unrelated task
A colleague repeats the same misconduct
Address the new incident and seek appropriate intervention
An employee feels tempted to retaliate
Avoid retaliation and use appropriate reporting channels
Trust remains damaged after repeated problems
Maintain reasonable boundaries and look for consistent improvement

sections.title: Day 5 — Lessons 3–7 Knowledge Assessment
paragraphs: Complete the 10-question knowledge check at the bottom of this lesson. It covers Lessons 3–7. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the best way to address a colleague's mistake? Attack the colleague's personality / Identify the specific issue and expected improvement / Discuss the mistake with everyone

What should you do when a colleague invites you to spread an unverified rumour? Avoid participating and redirect genuine concerns appropriately / Share the rumour with trusted friends / Post it in the staff group

Which action may constitute retaliation? Following an agreed handover procedure / Respectfully asking for clarification / Deliberately withholding necessary work information because a colleague reported a concern

When should an employee involve a supervisor? Whenever a colleague disagrees with them / When a repeated problem remains unresolved or a serious concern requires intervention / Only after a public argument
How should an immediate client safety concern be handled? Address the danger and escalate promptly / Wait until the end of the week / Discuss it only with friends

Why should individual disagreements generally be discussed privately when appropriate? To prevent any official record / To avoid all accountability / To protect dignity and encourage constructive communication

What should employees do during a private conflict-resolution conversation? Listen, clarify facts and agree on practical next steps / Concentrate on proving who is superior / Bring unrelated past mistakes into the discussion
What does moving forward after a disagreement require? Becoming close personal friends / Maintaining appropriate professional cooperation and agreed improvements / Ignoring repeated misconduct
What is the most reliable way to rebuild damaged trust? Demand immediate forgiveness / Make promises without changing behaviour / Demonstrate consistent honesty, reliability and improvement

Which statement best reflects Zura Spa's conflict-resolution expectations? Address issues fairly, avoid retaliation, seek help when needed and maintain respect / Support friends regardless of the facts / Avoid reporting serious misconduct to preserve peace

sections.title: Final personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain why workplace issues should be addressed without attacking personalities.
Describe three ways personal attacks can make conflict worse.
Explain the difference between gossip and legitimate reporting.
Give three examples of workplace retaliation.
Explain why friendship should not determine whose side you take during a conflict.
Identify five situations that may require supervisory intervention.
Describe how you would report a repeated workplace problem professionally.
Explain why private discussion can be more effective than public confrontation.
Explain what it means to move forward after a disagreement.
Describe how trust can be rebuilt after a colleague repeatedly fails to fulfil responsibilities.
Explain why moving forward does not mean abandoning accountability.

sections.title: Seven-day conflict-resolution challenge
table: Address work-related issues without personal insults
Refuse to participate in gossip or rumours
Avoid taking sides without understanding the facts
Identify when a concern requires supervisory assistance
Practise resolving a minor disagreement respectfully
Maintain professional cooperation with colleagues after disagreements
Reflect on one conflict-management habit you have improved

sections.title: Final Day 5 takeaway
paragraphs: Conflict is not always avoidable, but unnecessary hostility can often be prevented.

At Zura Spa, employees are expected to address genuine problems without personal attacks, avoid gossip and retaliation, seek supervisory assistance when appropriate, resolve concerns respectfully and maintain professional cooperation after disagreements.

The goal is not to create a workplace where nobody ever disagrees. The goal is to build a team where disagreements are handled fairly, responsibly and without damaging the service we provide to clients.
Next module: Day 6 — Accountability, Reliability and Supporting Colleagues.

remember: A strong team is not one where disagreements never happen. It is one where employees can disagree without becoming enemies, correct problems without humiliating one another, seek help without fear of retaliation and move forward with greater understanding, accountability and respect.
